Trachelyopterus fisheri (Eigenmann, 1916). Common name: Fisher's Woodcat. Type locality: Río Sucio, Colombia. Size: 28 cm SL (280 mm or 11").

Etymology: Trachelyopterus comes from the Greek trachelos, meaning neck, and pteron, meaning fin, in reference to the long cranial shield, which gives the appearance that the dorsal fin originates at the neck region. The specific epithet honours the American entrepreneur Carl Graham Fisher.

Identification: this is by far the most slender of all Trachelyopterus species. Another identifying feature is the terminal mouth, whereas other Trachelyopterus species have a slightly superior mouth.

South America: Sucio River basin. Colombia Caribbean Rivers, Atrato, Sucio.

IUCN Red List category: Least Concern (last assessed 2014).
Large pieces of driftwood as hiding places. See to it that there is also plenty of swimming space. The aquarium shouldn't be too brightly lit.

This species is not shy and can regularly be seen during the day, especially when being fed. All prepared and frozen foods are taken. Like all Auchenipterids, being surface feeders, they are particularly fond of insects and their larvae.

Despite their size these fish are very gentle, social and peaceful. Smaller fish may, however, be eaten, because they rest at night while these woodcats are on the move.

Suggested tankmates: non-aggressive fish and fishes that aren't too small.

Males have a genital papilla, thickened maxillary barbels, spawning tubercles on the barbels and on top of the head, and a curved, enlarged dorsal spine which can be moved up and forward. Their nape is also bent upwards, as can be seen in Tetranematichthys and Ageneiosus species. Females grow larger and display a plainer colour pattern.

Has been recorded (see Reference notes). Like other Auchenipterids, these fish have internal fertilization. The bodies are wrapped around each other, and to stay in position the male uses its barbels, dorsal spine and spawning tubercles. The actual mating lasts about 30 seconds or less. Four weeks later the female lays her eggs. The parents neither look after their eggs nor eat them.

In terms of general captive behaviour, this species doesn't resemble its congeners, but is more easily compared to the larger Auchenipterichthys and smaller ageneiosids. It is a very gentle species that glides through the water and never displays the hastiness so typical of other members of its genus. Moreover, the nape and the enlarged dorsal spine make it look more like an Ageneiosus or a Tetranematichthys.

See also TFH August 1982, pages 84-89, Burgess and Azuma: The first spawning of the woodcat, Trachycorystes insignis [sic]. The same pictures and a very short summary of the article can be found in An Atlas of Marine and Freshwater Catfishes (1989), pages 586-589, Burgess. In this book, the species is called Parauchenipterus fisheri, which was the correct name at the time.
Annals of the Carnegie Museum v. 10 (nos 1-2) (art. 6), pp 82.
